source_refs.note: Book p. 205-206: 11.4.1 Graphs of Trigonometric Functions: the five plotting steps (i)-(v), steps (iv)-(v) on p. 206, 'smooth curves' in bold.

blocks.text: To plot the graph we shall follow these steps:

items: (i) Table of ordered pairs \((x, y)\) is constructed, when \(x\) is the measure of the angle and \(y\) is the value of the trigonometric function for the angle of measure \(x\);
(ii) The measures of the angles are taken along the \(X\)-axis;
(iii) The values of the trigonometric functions are taken along the \(Y\)-axis;
(iv) The points corresponding to the ordered pairs are plotted on the graph paper;
(v) These points are joined with the help of smooth curves.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: What is a graph of a function? Each angle \(x\) (the input) gives one value \(y\) (the output). The pair \((x, y)\) is one point on graph paper. For example, \(\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5\) gives the point \((30^{\circ}, 0.5)\) on the graph of \(y = \sin x\). When we plot many such points and join them, the picture shows how the value of the function changes as the angle grows.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Degrees or radians on the \(X\)-axis? Both are used. Since \(\pi\) radians \(= 180^{\circ}\), every degree mark has a radian name. The tables in the next sub-sections give both, e.g. \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) or \(30^{\circ}\):

blocks.caption: Degree and radian names of the main marks on the X-axis (our table)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why smooth curves and not straight lines with a ruler? The value of a trigonometric function changes gradually between our plotted points. Example: the straight segment from \((30^{\circ}, 0.5)\) to \((60^{\circ}, 0.87)\) has middle height about \(0.68\), but the true value at \(45^{\circ}\) is \(\sin 45^{\circ} \approx 0.71\). The real graph bends above the straight line, so we join the points freehand with one smooth curve.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In a graph question marks are given for: a stated scale, labelled axes (\(X\) and \(Y\), with the angle marks), correctly plotted points, a smooth curve, and a title such as 'Graph of \(y = \sin x\)'. Use a sharp pencil and draw the curve in one go.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Make a table of ordered pairs \((x, y)\) first.
2. Angles go along the \(X\)-axis, function values along the \(Y\)-axis.
3. Plot the points, then join them with a smooth curve.
4. \(\pi\) radians \(= 180^{\circ}\); the \(X\)-axis may be marked in either unit.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Joining the points with a ruler: the graph becomes a zig-zag with sharp corners, which a trigonometric graph never has.
2. Putting the values on the \(X\)-axis and the angles on the \(Y\)-axis.
3. Unequal spacing of the angle marks: \(30^{\circ}\) steps must be equal distances.
